Create a temporary image $I_\theta$ of the same dimensions as $I$, initialized to zero.
Calculate the kernel weight $\Lambda(\phi=0, \rho, i, j)$ for every pixel $(i, j)$ in $I_\theta$ using the formula below.
Note that for the optimization step, the kernel is calculated assuming $\phi=0$ (horizontal/vertical alignment).
Add the contribution $p(\theta, \rho) \times \Lambda(\phi=0, \rho, i, j)$ to $I_\theta(i, j)$.
Rotate the temporary image $I_\theta$ by the angle $-\theta$.
Add the rotated $I_\theta$ to the result image $I$.

For each projection, it requires $O(N_\rho \cdot N_{pixels})$ for the backprojection into the temporary image, plus $O(N_{pixels})$ for the rotation and accumulation.
The rotation step dominates if implemented naively, but can be optimized.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Requires an additional temporary image of size $O(N_{pixels})$ per projection angle, or a single temporary image reused for all angles.
*   **When to Use:** When high geometric fidelity is required and subsampling artifacts are a concern, and computational resources allow for the rotation step.
